sentence: NASA's Space Launch System rocket and Orion spacecraft form the backbone for the agency's Artemis missions to the Moon.
Over development, the rocket and spacecraft moved from design and manufacturing to testing, assembly, and integration, with some hardware delivered to the launch pad at Kennedy.
The SLS core stage was built at Michoud Assembly Facility — the largest rocket stage NASA has built since the Saturn V, 212 feet tall, with four RS-25 engines.
SLS will be the most powerful rocket ever built, powered by two solid rocket boosters and four RS-25 engines providing over 8 million pounds of thrust.
SLS rolled out to Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy and was stacked inside the Vehicle Assembly Building ahead of its first flight.
At 1:47 a.m. EST (6:47 UTC) on November 16, 2022, NASA's Orion spacecraft launched atop the SLS rocket from historic Launch Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center.
The liftoff officially began the Artemis I mission — an uncrewed flight test.
Artemis I was the first integrated test of the agency's deep space exploration systems: the SLS rocket, the Orion spacecraft, and supporting ground systems.
It was the first in a series of increasingly complex missions to the Moon.
Orion was sent on a path to the Moon, beginning a 25.5-day mission around the Moon.
This was an uncrewed flight test demonstrating the SLS rocket's ability to carry Orion around the Moon and back to Earth.
Over the course of the mission, Orion performed two lunar flybys, coming within 80 miles (129 kilometers) of the lunar surface.
At its farthest distance during the mission, Orion traveled nearly 270,000 miles (435,000 kilometers) from Earth.
NASA's Orion spacecraft completed a parachute-assisted splashdown in the Pacific Ocean at 9:40 a.m. PST (12:40 p.m. EST).
Splashdown marked the final major milestone of the Artemis I mission.
Artemis I set new records of performance, exceeded efficiency expectations, and established new safety baselines for humans in deep space.
Following Artemis I, human beings will fly around the Moon on Artemis II.
Under Artemis, NASA will land the first woman and the first person of color on the Moon.
SLS, Orion, and the Gateway in lunar orbit form NASA's backbone for deep space exploration.
SLS is the only rocket that can send Orion, astronauts, and supplies to the Moon in a single mission.
